Let’s go back to the iris data set. Suppose that a flower with a Petal Length larger than 4 is considered a large flow.

Extension

title: Finish Loops and if else logic
Finish Loops and if else logic
text:
Vectorized operations
– if / else - operate on one value (so we need to iterate with a for loop)
– In R, vectorized means that a function can OPERATE on a whole vector of values at once, instead of requiring you to process each value individually with a loop (ifelse)

title: Finish Loops and if else logic
text:
Example
– mean(): not vectorized. It takes a vector as an input and produces a value. It does not operate on the entire vector
– round(): rounds each value in a vector. “Does something independently to each element”. This is consider vectorized!

title: Finish Loops and if else logic
text:
Test yourself
Which functions are vectorized?

x <- c(2,4,6)

length(x)

sqrt(x)

unique(x)

x > 2

title: Finish Loops and if else logic
text:
ifelse
Pull up the help file for ifelse
Now, create a new variable in the iris data set for the Sepal.Size. Have it say “Large” if the value is above 5.5, and “Small” for anything else.

title: Finish Loops and if else logic
text:
Solution

iris$Sepal.Size <- ifelse(
  iris$Sepal.Length > 5.5,
  "Large",
  "Small"
)

YAML
We have mappings and keys!

R Objects
When we create something in R, such as a number, a word, or a collection of values, R stores it as an object.

Vectors
A vector is a collection of values.
c stands for combine (you can think about this as collection if you would like!)

title: Quarto II & Objects/Vectors/Lists
text:
Summary
The components (variables) of a data frame have to be the same length! Lists, they do not.
A data frame is designed for: Many observations of the same set of variables.
A list is designed for: Putting different kinds of information together.
Or: A list organizes objects; a data frame organizes observations into rows and variables into columns.

title: Error Making PDFs / Trouble Rendering
text:
These are questions to ask yourself / check if you are having trouble rendering your document.
– Do you have TinyTex installed? In order to render PDF documents, you need to install the PDF compiler. You can do this by running tinytex::install_tinytex() in your Console.
– Are my code chunk labels weird? To create a code chunk label, you need the following #| label: at the start of your code chunk. If you have spaces in the name you put, or if you are using special characters, you may not be able to render your document.
– Does your code run? If you have errors in your code, you will also have errors when rendering the document.
– Did you put View() in a code chunk? We don’t use View often, but we need to be aware that any function that calls for an external viewer will break the render.

title: Instructor + course overview
text:
Dr. Elijah Meyer - Hello! I’m very excited to work with you all this semester. I’ve earned a Master’s degree in statistics and a Ph.D. in statistics with a focus in education from Montana State University, and completed a teaching post-doc position at Duke University. My early research is in sports statistics, with an emphasis on spatial data visualizations to enhance sports strategy. My current work is in statistics/data science education. My focus is on improving the educational experience for both instructors and students. Current projects include creating a dynamic interactive shiny application in R to better students’ understanding of statistics and data science; exploring interest-driven assessment, and creating an national data science assessment around reasoning.
My student led projects include: 3D Printed Geometric Structures with Liquid Metal as Flexible Sensors, & An assessment of wildlife use of rhododendron in western North Carolina.
Prior to my time at NC State, I’ve taught multiple sections of Introductory Data Science at Duke University, and Introductory and Intermediate Statistics at Montana State. At Montana State, I developed their Intermediate Statistics online course, and helped integrate R into the Introductory Statistics curricula.
I prioritize community, communication, and respect in my classroom. I want to provide a space where we can freely talk about the material, embrace mistakes, and learn together throughout the semester.
When I’m not in the books, I enjoy playing disc golf, tennis, basketball, and anything else that gets me outside and active. I’m looking forward to meeting you all and having a great semester!

Go to https://github.com/, and create an account (unless you already have one).
Some tips from Happy Git with R.
– Incorporate your actual name!

Source vs Visual
– Source tab shows raw plain-text markdown and code

title: Intro to Quarto
text:
YAML
We have mappings and keys!
You can think of the “map” as a YAML option. You can think of the “key” as the value the option takes on.
---
title: "My Document"
---
title is the “map” and “My Document” is the key!
Note: When we are working with a simple string, the quotes are optional. When you are working with things likes numbers that you want to be treated as text, quotes are necessary.
Options

text:
YAML
What’s the difference?


Example 1
---
title: "Test Document"
author:
name: Elijah Meyer
affiliation: NC State University
---
Example 2
---
title: "Test Document"
author:
- name: Elijah Meyer
affiliation: NC State University
---

Example 3
---
title: "Test Document"
author:
  - name: Elijah Meyer
    affiliation: NC State University
---

title: Intro to Quarto
text:
YAML
The - is necessary when we have a list item (an item that we could have multiple of)
author
  └── list item
        ├── name
        └── affiliation
Most (not all) YAML headings require indentation. This is a good habit to get into early.

For Loop
Define each piece of the for loop below, to help us uncover the definition

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
for -
x -
in -
1:3 -
{ } -
print(x) -

title: Finish Lists and Loops
text:
For Loop

for (x in 1:3) {
  print(x)
}

for - tells R to repeat something
x - the current number
in - tells R where to get the numbers from
1:3 - the numbers R goes through: 1, 2, 3
{ } - contains what R should repeat
print(x) - prints the current number

student <- list(

  age = 19,
  scores = c(92, 88, 95)
)

for (x in student) {

}

[1] 19
